newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major attacks Labour over Europe.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major attacks Labour over Europe.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major trained his fire on the Labour party's European policy on Thursday, accusing opposition leader Tony Blair of threatening to put jobs at risk.

Buoyant after a poll which showed his ruling Conservatives closing the gap with Labour, Major attacked Blair's pledge to sign up to the European Social Chapter, saying it was the result of a secret deal with the unions.

"If Mr Blair signed the Social Chapter, Britain would be powerless to stop policies that have helped create the worst dole queues in post-war Europe being injected into Britain," Major told supporters during a tour round central England.
Major said the unions, whose powers have been drastically curbed in 18 years of unbroken Conservative rule, were waiting for a payoff for the funds they contributed to the Labour party.

"The unions have long seen Europe as the backdoor to power in Britain. While (former premier) Margaret Thatcher and I have been in charge, that backdoor has stayed firmly bolted. A Labour government would slip that bolt ever so quietly open," Major said.

Major's speech was the highpoint of a campaign day which took him to a booming outdoor clothing manufacturer in Nottingham and the Rocester headquarters of the JCB earth-moving machinery firm, owned by Conservative supporter Sir Anthony Bamford.

Aides said Major's decision to focus on the Social Chapter, which sets minimum levels of workers' rights across the union but which Britain has opted out of, was designed to increase pressure on Blair before the launch of a Labour business manifesto on Friday.
Blair is expected to say he will not allow the Social Chapter to reduce the flexibility of Britain's labour market by introducing the kind of regulations seen in Germany, France or Spain.
But Major said Blair could do this by introducing laws in Britain's parliament without signing up for the Social Chapter.

"If Mr Blair is not willing to do that, why not?... Is he afraid of parliamentary decision? Does he trust Brussels more than Westminster?" Major told around 500 supporters who filled a hall at the JCB plant for an evening rally.
Major's decision to widen the attack to Europe, a subject which has dogged his efforts to unite the party in the run-up to the campaign for the May 1 election, underlined his growing confidence.
Conservative strategists have been delighted at what they see as successful attacks on Labour over a recent U-turn on privatisation.

Accusing Labour of a "panic" conversion to privatisation to fill a gaping hole in their spending plans, Major told several hundred delighted supporters: "Why are we in such good spirits today? Because we've seen that the Labour party crumble, crumple and crash to the ground under the first bit of real pressure."

Major, clearly bolstered by the friendly crowds awaiting him as he tours the country, has been cheered by a MORI poll in Thursday's Times which showed a sharp 12-point fall in Labour's lead in a week.
Telling his supporters to "fight clean, but fight like terriers", Major said: "In the next three weeks the Conservative party will write the biggest news story in modern political history."

But the MORI poll still gives Labour 49 points to 34 for the Conservatives, and a daily Gallup poll in Thursday's Telegraph newspaper showed Labour's lead up four points on the day before to 23, leaving Major a mountain to climb to win the election.

Major, however, is convinced that Labour's lead can be undermined by stressing Blair's lack of experience in government and taking aim at the opposition leader's appeal to voters to trust his party despite a lack of dramatic campaign promises.
